text: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.[fn]

versions.text: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
versions.explanation: The words "the Son of God" are absent from the base text used here (some early manuscripts lack them). A brief footnote such as "Some manuscripts do not include 'the Son of God.'" would inform the reader without altering the reading text.

text: As it is written in the prophet Isaiah: "See, I am sending my messenger ahead of you, who will prepare your way"—
"A voice cries out in the wilderness: 'Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.'"

versions.text: "a voice of one calling in the wilderness: 'Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight'"—
versions.explanation: The trailing em dash leads into a new sentence in verse 4 ("John appeared..."), which reads awkwardly aloud and leaves the quotation grammatically unfinished. Closing the citation cleanly, and using a finite verb, improves oral flow while keeping the sense.

text: John appeared in the wilderness, baptizing and proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.
The whole Judean countryside went out to him, and all the people of Jerusalem, and they were baptized by him in the Jordan River, confessing their sins.
John was clothed in camel's hair with a leather belt around his waist, and he ate locusts and wild honey.
And he proclaimed: "After me comes one mightier than I, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to stoop down and untie.
I have baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit."
In those days Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan.
And just as he was coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens torn open and the Spirit, like a dove, coming down on him.

versions.text: And just as he was coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens torn open and the Spirit descending on him like a dove.
versions.explanation: In the current word order "on him like a dove" can be heard as comparing him, rather than the Spirit, to a dove. Placing the comparison next to "the Spirit" follows the Greek order and removes the ambiguity when read aloud.

text: And a voice came from heaven: "You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased."
At once the Spirit drove him out into the wilderness.
He was in the wilderness forty days, tempted by Satan. He was with the wild animals, and the angels served him.
After John was arrested, Jesus came into Galilee proclaiming the gospel of God.
"The time has been fulfilled," he said, "and the kingdom of God has come near. Repent, and believe in the gospel."
As he walked along the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and his brother Andrew casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.
Jesus said to them, "Come, follow me, and I will make you fishers of men."
At once they left their nets and followed him.
Going on a little farther, he saw James son of Zebedee and his brother John, in their boat mending the nets.
He called them at once, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men and went off after him.
They went into Capernaum, and right away, on the Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and began to teach.
They were astounded at his teaching, for he taught them as one who had authority, not as the scribes.
Just then, in their synagogue, there was a man with an unclean spirit, and he cried out,
"What do you want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God!"
But Jesus rebuked him: "Be silent, and come out of him!"
The unclean spirit convulsed the man, shrieked with a loud voice, and came out of him.
They were all so amazed that they debated among themselves: "What is this? A new teaching—and with authority! He even commands the unclean spirits, and they obey him."
And news about him spread at once through the whole surrounding region of Galilee.
As soon as they left the synagogue, they went with James and John to the house of Simon and Andrew.
Simon's mother-in-law was lying sick with a fever, and they told him about her at once.
He went to her, took her by the hand, and raised her up. The fever left her, and she began to serve them.
That evening, after sunset, they brought to him all who were sick and those possessed by demons.
The whole town was gathered at the door.
He healed many who were sick with various diseases and drove out many demons; and he would not let the demons speak, because they knew him.
Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he got up, went out to a solitary place, and prayed there.
Simon and those with him went searching for him,
and when they found him they said, "Everyone is looking for you."
He said to them, "Let us go elsewhere, to the neighboring towns, so that I may preach there too. That is why I came."
So he went throughout all Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and driving out demons.
A man with leprosy came to him, begging on his knees: "If you are willing, you can make me clean."
Moved with compassion, Jesus reached out his hand and touched him. "I am willing," he said. "Be clean."[fn]

versions.text: Moved with compassion, Jesus reached out his hand and touched him. "I am willing," he said. "Be clean."
versions.explanation: The base Greek text here reads ὀργισθείς ("filled with indignation/anger"), while "moved with compassion" renders the variant σπλαγχνισθείς. Since the reading text follows the compassion variant, a footnote is needed, e.g. "Some manuscripts read 'filled with indignation.'" Otherwise readers lose an important textual difference.

text: Immediately the leprosy left him, and he was clean.
Jesus sent him away at once with a stern warning:
"See that you say nothing to anyone. Go, show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, as a testimony to them."

But the man went out and began to proclaim it freely, spreading the word so widely that Jesus could no longer enter a town openly, but stayed outside in lonely places. And people came to him from everywhere.
